sources.title: Angelica Kauffman (Q123098), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-20): English label 'Angelika Kauffmann', description 'Swiss artist (1741-1807)', Korean label 앙겔리카 카우프만, human, born 30 October 1741, died 5 November 1807, citizenship Switzerland, occupations include painter. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

National Gallery, London, artist page 'Angelica Kauffmann (1741-1807)' (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls her one of the most celebrated artists of the eighteenth century, educated in Rome, who made history paintings; only child of the painter Joseph Johann Kauffmann; unable to enrol at an academy as a woman, so she studied ancient and modern art with her father; elected to the Accademia di San Luca in Rome at 23 but not allowed to attend its meetings or draw from live models; moved to London in 1766, friend of Joshua Reynolds, one of only two women founding members of the Royal Academy in 1768; made her income mainly from portraits but defined herself as a history painter and exhibited history paintings there every year; moved to Rome in 1782 where her studio and salon were a stop for Grand Tourists; died in Rome in 1807. Museum summary, admiring.

Royal Academy of Arts, 'Start here: Angelica Kauffman' (exhibition introduction, 24 January 2024; read in full): child prodigy trained by her father, travelled with him in Italy, portraits of Grand Tour visitors, the Winckelmann and Garrick portraits, move to London in 1766, one of two women among the 36 founding members in 1768 (the women could not attend committee meetings or dinners or work from life models), ambitious history paintings with female protagonists, the four ceiling paintings 'Elements of Art' unveiled in 1780 with all four stages of making a picture shown as women, left London in 1781-82 for Rome, funeral in Rome and a bust placed in the Pantheon beside Raphael's. Institutional exhibition copy for the Academy of which she was a founder, so admiring.

Jenny Uglow, 'The meteoric rise of Angelica Kauffman RA', RA Magazine / Royal Academy of Arts (2 January 2024; read in full). Historian's account: her October 1766 letter to her father from London, the Garrick portrait she had sent ahead to a London exhibition, her portraits and history paintings, her female-centred treatment of Ulysses subjects, the fashionable sentimental and Oriental paintings she produced, the 1767 marriage to the fraudster Count de Horn, her marriage to Antonio Zucchi in 1781, the 1778-80 'Elements of Art' commission and the Rome salon; says she played to the prevailing tune of fashion and negotiated, and even exploited, her position as a woman artist.

Alexandra Harris, 'Angelica Kauffman: Art History's Heroine', RA Magazine / Royal Academy of Arts (4 April 2024; read in full). Long-form essay: her reputation was made in London in 1766-81 and she worked in Rome 'with astonishing energy and dedication' until she could no longer hold a brush; she and Reynolds advocated history painting; her Penelope and Eleanor subjects centre women; her engravings reached ordinary homes; Goethe's year of Sunday gallery visits with her in 1787-88 and his remark that her eye was highly trained and her feeling for the beautiful, true and tender great; also calls her portraits 'smooth flattery' that omitted anything Reynolds called accidental deformity.

Amy Bluett, 'Mary Moser and Angelica Kauffman: the RA's founding women', Royal Academy of Arts (archive-based article, 2 March 2021; read in full): her 1768 signature on the petition to George III for a Royal Academy, the limits placed on its two women founders (no committee meetings or dinners), and the text of her 1775 letter to the President and Council protesting against the exhibition of Nathaniel Hone's The Conjuror and offering to withdraw from the Academy, after which the Hanging Committee removed the picture.

National Museum of Women in the Arts, artist profile 'Angelica Kauffman' (read in full): child prodigy producing commissioned portraits in her early teens, trained by her father, travelled through Switzerland, Austria and Italy as his assistant and copied classical and Renaissance works, election to the Accademia di San Luca in 1765, success in London, exhibited at the Royal Academy for sixteen years, married Antonio Zucchi who became her business manager, funeral directed by Canova on the model of Raphael's. Short museum profile, admiring.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Angelica Kauffmann' (read in full): early Rococo influences, Italian visits in 1754 and 1763 and the influence of Mengs's Neoclassicism, invited to London in 1766 by Lady Wentworth, favoured by the royal family, signatory of the petition for the Royal Academy and one of two women founding members, work in the 1770s on painted decorations for interiors designed by Robert Adam, retirement to Rome in the early 1780s with her second husband Antonio Zucchi; judges her mythological compositions Rococo in tone with Neoclassical poses and her portraits of women among her best. Short reference article.

Frances A. Gerard, 'Angelica Kauffmann: A Biography' (London: Ward and Downey, 1893 edition; Internet Archive scan, OCR read in part: the chapters on the Horn marriage and separation, the 1775 Hone dispute, her refusal of offers to stay at the Neapolitan court, her clothing of nude subjects, the 1781 press criticism and the 1798 war losses). Victorian biography built on letters and on the 1810 life by de Rossi, admiring in tone and sometimes moralising; used for the contemporary critic who said she seemed to have copied pictures, prints and plaster casts rather than living models, and for her own letters and refusals. Partly derivative of earlier biographers.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_kauffman_ng, src_kauffman_nmwa, src_kauffman_ra_start, src_kauffman_gerard | 1750s-1760s | museum summary, museum profile, institutional exhibition copy, biography] Four sources agree she was trained by her father, copied classical sculptures and Old Masters in the Italian galleries, and made history painting rather than only portraits her stated field; she was elected to the Accademia di San Luca at 23 although shut out of its life classes. Most of the training was arranged by her father, and a 1781 critic quoted by Gerard said her figures looked copied from pictures, prints and plasters, so the score stays moderate. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.58 to 64 / 0.50 because the training was directed by her father and the accounts largely repeat one museum-world narrative.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_kauffman_ra_uglow, src_kauffman_ra_bluett, src_kauffman_britannica | 1765-1768 | historian's article, archive-based institutional article, reference biography] Uglow says she had arranged an introduction in advance by sending her Garrick portrait to a London exhibition in 1765, and Bluett and Britannica agree she signed the 1768 petition for a Royal Academy. She also accepted Lady Wentworth's invitation to London in 1766, separating from her father. The advance introduction rests on one historian's reading, and the move was an invitation. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.56 to 62 / 0.50 because the advance-planning claim is a single historian's interpretation and two of the three sources are Royal Academy material.

achievement_drive.rationale: [src_kauffman_ra_uglow, src_kauffman_ng, src_kauffman_ra_harris | 1766-1807 | historian's article, museum summary, long-form essay] Uglow says portraits made her rich yet she was ambitious to reach higher, the National Gallery says she defined herself as a history painter and exhibited history paintings at the Academy every year, and Harris says she was constantly in demand and worked with astonishing energy for four decades. The ambition is a modern writer's characterisation, with little of her own stated aim. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.54 to 62 / 0.46 and from strong inference to inference because the drive is described by recent writers, not shown in her own words, and two of the three sources are Royal Academy material.

persistence.rationale: [src_kauffman_ra_harris, src_kauffman_nmwa, src_kauffman_gerard | 1769-1807 | long-form essay, museum profile, biography] Harris says she worked in Rome until she could no longer hold a brush and was in demand for four decades, the museum profile says she exhibited at the Academy for sixteen years, and Gerard quotes her 1798-1800 letters about war losses and a suspended German market while she kept working on a commission. Output and demand are partly outcomes of fame, not direct evidence of perseverance. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.50 to 58 / 0.44 and from strong inference to inference because the main claim is one essay's summary and exhibition record counts output more than persistence.

adaptability.rationale: [src_kauffman_ra_uglow, src_kauffman_britannica, src_kauffman_nmwa, src_kauffman_ng | 1750s-1782 | historian's article, reference biography, museum profile, museum summary] She worked in Switzerland, Austria, Italy and England, moved her career from Italy to London in 1766 and back to Rome in 1782, took on decorative schemes for Adam interiors alongside portraits and history paintings, and Uglow says she followed the prevailing sentimental, classical and Oriental fashions. The fashion-following claim is one historian's reading. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.52 to 60 / 0.50 because the fashion-following claim rests on one source.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_kauffman_ra_bluett, src_kauffman_gerard | 1775 | archive-based institutional article, biography] In 1775 she wrote to the Academy's President and Council protesting against the exhibition of Hone's The Conjuror, which was said to ridicule her alleged relationship with Reynolds, and offered to withdraw her pictures; the Hanging Committee removed it. Gerard tells the same episode and adds that she shrank from notoriety and that Hone later wrote to her. One documented episode over a personal slight, in a career otherwise marked by tact. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.50 to 56 / 0.46 because it is one episode told by two accounts, and the second is Victorian and drawn from the same record.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_kauffman_ra_uglow, src_kauffman_ra_harris, src_kauffman_britannica, src_kauffman_gerard | 1764-1788 | historian's article, long-form essay, reference biography, biography] Uglow and Harris say she centred women in subjects usually told through male heroes (Penelope, Ulysses scenes) and in 1780 showed all four stages of making a picture as women; against this, Britannica calls her mythological work Rococo in tone with Neoclassical poses, Uglow says she played to fashion, and a 1781 critic quoted by Gerard said she copied pictures and prints. The originality claim comes from two Royal Academy writers and is contested. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.46 to 54 / 0.40 and from strong inference to inference because both supporting sources are Royal Academy material and independent sources point the other way.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_kauffman_ra_harris | 1787-1788 | long-form essay] Harris quotes Goethe, her friend and gallery companion in 1787-88, saying her eye was highly trained and she had enormous feeling for everything beautiful, true and tender, and describes the Sunday visits he made to galleries and churches with her. A single admiring contemporary judgment, reported through one essay. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.44 to 56 / 0.38 because it rests on one quotation relayed by one essay.

portrait.source: Half-tone plate captioned 'Portrait of Angelica Kauffman, painted by herself' (credit line 'Alinari, Photo. In the Uffizi, Florence') in Clara Erskine Clement Waters, Women in the Fine Arts from the Seventh Century B.C. to the Twentieth Century A.D. (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1904), Internet Archive scan womeninfineartsf00wate_0 (Boston Public Library copy; the record states no rights of its own). The plate reproduces her self-portrait in the Uffizi. The image is the plate area cropped from the 2182 x 3619 page scan and downscaled to 734 x 1000, with no upscaling.

I opened the Wikisource page and the Internet Archive page scan (leaf with the plate): the printed caption reads 'Portrait of Angelica Kauffman, painted by herself', with 'Alinari, Photo. In the Uffizi, Florence'. Basis: US publication 1904 (before 1931), underlying painter died 1807; no holder file used. KIND likeness: authentic self-portrait by the sitter, reproduced in a half-tone plate (visibly grainy; not a new rendering). CAVEATS for lead: (1) no Uffizi item record or Uffizi reuse terms were read because no Uffizi file is used (Italian cultural-heritage reproduction rules are theoretically relevant to the Uffizi's own images, not to a 1904 US book plate); (2) the Commons copy of this plate was not downloadable (429), so the image comes from the Internet Archive scan.
